sections.title: Cap and gills
sections.text: Tricholoma terreum (Schaeff.) P. Kumm., the grey knight, usually has a 4–8 cm mouse-grey to dark-grey cap, convex then expanded, sometimes with a low umbo. Its dry surface is downy to fibrillose; radial fibres may separate with age and reveal the pale flesh. The gills are fragile, whitish then pearl-grey, distant to moderately spaced, and notched near the stem.

sections.title: Stem, flesh and habitat
sections.text: The whitish to pale-grey stem is about 3–8 cm long, fibrous, and lacks a ring or volva. The flesh is pale, thin beneath the cap and does not change markedly when cut. The smell is faint, described as mild or slightly farinaceous by some sources. This ectomycorrhizal species is most often found beneath pines and other conifers; it fruits in groups from late summer through autumn, sometimes into early winter. The spore print is white.

sections.title: Look-alikes
sections.text: Several grey Tricholoma species look similar; colour or a photograph alone cannot separate them. Many sources treat Tricholoma myomyces as a synonym of T. terreum, although some authors still distinguish these concepts, including by whether a partial veil is present in young specimens. Characters and names vary among field guides. Reliable identification may require several characters or microscopic examination.

sections.title: Edibility and toxicological debate
sections.text: Published views do not fully agree. A 2014 study isolated compounds from specimens identified as T. terreum, some of which were toxic to mice; this prompted a mycotoxicological debate. The original authors defended their results in 2016, while mycologists disputed their interpretation. In 2024, a study of two ITS-identified Italian collections did not detect several previously reported compound families but did isolate saponaceolide B; its authors concluded that the specimens studied were edible. These limited findings do not provide a general safety guarantee. DGfM and VAPKO lists include the species among recommended mushrooms, but they do not replace secure identification. Never eat a mushroom identified only from this page or an image.

traits: Mouse-grey to dark-grey cap, usually 4–8 cm, dry, downy to fibrillose, sometimes with a low umbo
Fragile pale then pearl-grey gills, distant to moderately spaced and notched
Pale fibrous stem without ring or volva; thin pale flesh, little change when cut
White spore print; faint smell, sometimes described as slightly farinaceous
Ectomycorrhizal, often beneath pines and other conifers; groups in late summer and autumn
safetyNote: The food status is debated in toxicological literature: DGfM and VAPKO lists recommend it, while scientific studies report different findings depending on compounds and collections tested. This proves neither uniform toxicity nor universal safety. Do not eat a specimen without expert identification; grey Tricholoma species are easily confused.
